notes: Asylum interview tape recording JR; Court of Appeal held post-Mapah legal aid change created procedural unfairness.

enrichment.short_title: Dirshe: asylum interview tape recording after legal aid change
key_facts: Somali asylum seeker Dirshe sought to tape record his asylum interview after the Home Office refused the request.
Since 1 April 2004 legal aid generally no longer funded representatives or interpreters to attend asylum interviews.
The interview record is created by the interviewing officer and can be critical to credibility findings on appeal.
Pitchford J in Mapah had upheld the no-recording policy when funded attendance was available as a safeguard.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against refusal of permission for judicial review of the policy refusing tape recording of asylum interviews.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the court declared it unlawful to refuse tape recording where the applicant is not accompanied by a legal representative and/or interpreter.
enrichment.ratio: Where asylum applicants dependent on public funding can no longer practically have a representative or interpreter at interview, fairness requires an adequate means to challenge the officer's verbatim record; permitting a tape recording is the appropriate safeguard.
legal_issues: Whether the asylum interview procedure remained fair after legal aid changes removed funded attendance at interviews
Whether Mapah remained binding after the change in Immigration Contract Specification funding
Whether refusal to permit tape recording was irrational or procedurally unfair
What order should follow a finding of unfairness
linked_authorities: Mapah v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2003] EWHC 306 (Admin)
Secretary of State for the Home Department v Thirukumar [1989] Imm AR 402

confidence.notes: Policy change, fairness reasoning and declaratory order are clearly and fully explained.

notes: Liability trial on defective glass inspection machines; buyers held entitled to damages for repudiatory breach.

enrichment.short_title: Gregg v Emhart: defective glass cold-end inspection machines

statutes_considered.title: Sale and Supply of Goods Act 1994
Supply of Goods and Services Act 1982

key_facts: Gregg bought six automated glass inspection machines from Emhart for three cold-end lines at Knottingley in 1999.
Gregg and assignee Allied Glass contended the Prism 5000 and Scanner 8200 machines were defective in design and manufacture.
The machines operated in a hot, dirty environment near the hot end without an insulating barrier, which Emhart knew.
Repeated shutdowns and modification attempts continued until Gregg purported to reject the machines in May 2002.
enrichment.procedural_posture: First-stage Technology and Construction Court trial of liability only on buyers' Part 20 claim and seller's price claim.
enrichment.outcome: Allied Glass entitled to judgment with damages to be assessed; equipment was not of satisfactory quality or fit for purpose and Emhart repudiated the contract.
enrichment.ratio: Where cold-end inspection equipment supplied for a known harsh operating environment was not of satisfactory quality or fit for its known purpose, and Emhart failed adequately to diagnose and remedy faults, the buyer could accept repudiation and recover damages notwithstanding Emhart's exclusion clauses not being incorporated.
legal_issues: Whether there was one contract or three for the six machines
Whether implied terms as to quality and fitness were breached
Whether Emhart owed and breached a voluntary duty of care in diagnosis and remedial services
Whether the buyer lawfully rejected the goods or accepted repudiation and whether limitation clauses applied

confidence.notes: Detailed issue-list answers on liability are explicit though quantum was reserved.

notes: SENDISTAT appeal on blind dyslexic pupil placement; Walker J dismissed all grounds except settled IT issue.

enrichment.short_title: N's Parents v Somerset: special school placement appeal dismissed
key_facts: N, an 11-year-old registered blind pupil with dyslexia and cone dystrophy, was placed at mainstream Danesfield Middle School.
Her parents sought placement at the specialist West of England School in Exeter, about £10,000 per year more expensive.
The SENDISTAT dismissed their appeal against the amended Statement of Special Educational Needs in November 2004.
Parents challenged inadequate reasons, visual fatigue, literacy progress, Braille and emotional welfare findings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal under section 11 Tribunals and Inquiries Act 1992 from a SENDISTAT decision on a Statement of Special Educational Needs.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on all live grounds; the tribunal's reasons were sufficient and its mainstream placement decision was lawful.
enrichment.ratio: A SENDISTAT need only give summary reasons dealing with substantial points; comparing a visually impaired child's attainment gap with mainstream peers is not an appropriate basis for a statement finding, and failure to mention visual fatigue did not vitiate the decision in that context.
legal_issues: Whether the tribunal failed to give adequate reasons on visual fatigue and literacy progress
Whether the tribunal erred on Braille and specialist teaching needs
Whether Danesfield could meet N's needs so that WES was not appropriate under section 324
Whether rejection of evidence of unhappiness at school was irrational
linked_authorities: R v East Sussex County Council, ex parte Tandy [1998] AC 714
R (L) v London Borough of Waltham Forest [2003] EWHC 2907 (Admin)
J v Devon County Council [2001] EWHC Admin 958

confidence.notes: Ground-by-ground analysis and dismissal after agreement on the IT issue are comprehensively reasoned.

notes: GMC section 41A application; interim suspension extended 12 months after indecent assault conviction.

enrichment.short_title: GMC v Nammalwar: extension of interim suspension order
key_facts: Dr Nammalwar faced GMC proceedings after complaints of indecent assault and clinical competence concerns from 2003.
He was convicted of indecent assault in November 2004 and sentenced to three months' imprisonment.
The Interim Orders Panel replaced conditions with suspension on 17 March 2005; voluntary erasure was refused as against public interest.
The doctor did not consent to extending the interim suspension but had retired and did not intend to resume practice.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application by the General Medical Council under section 41A(7) Medical Act 1983 to extend an interim suspension order.
enrichment.outcome: Application granted; interim suspension extended for 12 months from 11 May 2005 to 10 May 2006 with £900 costs summarily assessed.
enrichment.ratio: Section 41A serves as a legitimate restraint on delay in fitness to practise proceedings; where a doctor has been convicted, does not intend to resume practice and the GMC has proceeded properly, the court may extend interim suspension for the maximum period.
legal_issues: Whether extension of the interim suspension order was appropriate
Effect of the doctor's conviction and voluntary erasure application
Whether the doctor's lack of consent prevented extension
Costs of the hearing

confidence.notes: Brief ex tempore judgment with clear facts, discretion exercised and costs order.

notes: Renewed permission application; Sedley LJ granted limited appeal on Article 3 distinct from Refugee Convention analysis.

enrichment.short_title: Ikaeva: permission to appeal on Article 3 asylum claim
key_facts: Mrs Ikaeva, from North Ossetia, claimed persecution linked to her husband's Chechen sympathies and hooligan attacks on her family.
The adjudicator found her account truthful but held there was no persecution and adequate state protection under Horvath.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal upheld the adjudicator on Refugee Convention grounds and internal relocation.
Her alternative Article 3 claim was dismissed in one sentence without separate analysis.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application to the Court of Appeal for permission to appeal after refusal on the papers by Buxton LJ.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted on the sole issue whether Article 3 was adequately dealt with; other grounds refused.
enrichment.ratio: Article 3 may require separate analysis from Refugee Convention persecution and Horvath state protection findings; rolling Article 3 together with persecution without distinct reasoning is arguably an error of law warranting permission.
legal_issues: Whether the IAT had jurisdiction over the appeal
Whether internal flight was a question of fact not law
Whether Article 3 was adequately considered separately from Refugee Convention persecution
Whether permission should be granted on any ground
linked_authorities: Horvath v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2000] UKHL 37

confidence.notes: Short permission judgment with clear limitation of the appeal issue and procedural order.

notes: Attorney General's Reference; community sentence for imitation firearm offence increased to 15 months.

enrichment.short_title: AG Ref No 155/2004: unduly lenient community sentence increased
key_facts: Deborah Martin pleaded guilty to unlawful wounding and possessing an imitation firearm with intent to cause fear of violence.
She and co-defendants attacked the Stephenson family at home at night, using a craft knife and an imitation handgun.
The Crown Court imposed a three-year community rehabilitation order with curfew on each count concurrently.
The Attorney General referred the sentence as unduly lenient for the firearms offence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's Reference under section 36 Criminal Justice Act 1988 alleging an unduly lenient sentence.
enrichment.outcome: Reference allowed; sentence increased to 15 months' imprisonment on both counts concurrently, with surrender to custody by noon the next day.
enrichment.ratio: A non-custodial sentence was unduly lenient for a premeditated home invasion involving an imitation firearm after group violence, but double jeopardy, prior non-custodial sentence and post-sentence progress justified a substantial reduction from the two-and-a-half to three years otherwise expected.
legal_issues: Whether the community sentence for the firearms offence was unduly lenient
Application of Avis, Hinchcliffe and Nixon sentencing guidance
Effect of double jeopardy and offender progress on the increased sentence
Appropriate surrender arrangements
linked_authorities: R v Avis [1998] 2 Cr App R (S) 178
Attorney General's Reference No 49 of 1999 (Hinchcliffe) [2000] 1 Cr App R (S) 436
Attorney General's Reference No 71 of 2001 (Nixon) [2002] 2 Cr App R (S) 79

confidence.notes: Facts, aggravating features, authorities and substituted sentence are clearly stated.

notes: Asbestos mesothelioma preliminary issues; breach and causation found and section 33 limitation disapplied.

enrichment.short_title: Smith v MoD: asbestos mesothelioma and limitation disapplied
key_facts: George Smith died of mesothelioma in 1991 after asbestos exposure at RAF Coningsby between 1960 and 1962.
His widow learned of the MoD exposure only in May 1995 from former colleague Frank Ward.
She instructed solicitors but abandoned the claim after poor advice, threatening cost letters and legal aid withdrawal in 1995.
Proceedings were commenced in 2004 after a 2002 television programme prompted fresh advice.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of preliminary issues on breach, causation and limitation in a mesothelioma claim against the Ministry of Defence.
enrichment.outcome: Claimant succeeded on breach, causation and section 33; primary limitation period disapplied and claim may proceed.
enrichment.ratio: Where a widow acted promptly when she learned of exposure but reasonably abandoned pursuit because solicitors gave no encouragement and threatened costs, and defendants suffered no material prejudice from delay, section 33 may disapply limitation despite a heavy burden especially where liability is strong.
legal_issues: Whether the MoD breached statutory and common law duties as to asbestos exposure
Whether exposure at Coningsby caused Mr Smith's mesothelioma
When the primary limitation period started and expired
Whether section 33 should disapply limitation given delay and solicitor conduct
linked_authorities: KR v Bryn Alyn Community (Holdings) Ltd [2003] EWCA Civ 85
Buckler v JF Finnegan Ltd [2004] EWCA Civ 920

confidence.notes: Detailed section 33 analysis on unusual solicitor-related delay with clear preliminary issue findings.

notes: Parole Board JR; decision quashed for insufficient reasons on protected witness resettlement risk reduction.

enrichment.short_title: Tinney v Parole Board: parole refusal quashed for inadequate reasons
key_facts: Tinney received eight years for a prolonged armed robbery career but gave Crown evidence against dangerous co-offenders.
He entered witness protection, was isolated in custody and faced serious reprisal risk on release.
Prison and probation reports unanimously supported parole with intensive supervision and resettlement away from old associates.
The Parole Board refused parole in September 2004, saying good behaviour did not show risk had reduced to a safe level.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review with permission to quash a Parole Board decision refusing early release on licence.
enrichment.outcome: Decision quashed as insufficiently reasoned; fresh panel hearing ordered within four weeks with best endeavours for updated probation evidence.
enrichment.ratio: Following Oyston, a parole refusal letter must explain in broad terms why factors pointing against risk, including protected witness status and resettlement away from old haunts, did not reduce risk to a safe level; bare reliance on good behaviour not reducing risk is inadequate in this unusual case.
legal_issues: Whether the Parole Board irrationally found no reduction in reoffending risk
Whether Secretary of State directions on public safety were properly applied
Whether reasons were adequate under Oyston
Appropriate remedy and timetable for reconsideration
linked_authorities: R v Parole Board, ex parte Oyston [2000] 1 March (unreported)

confidence.notes: Detailed background reports, Oyston analysis and quashing order are clearly reasoned.

notes: Consolidated Iraq protest appeals; aggravated trespass and criminal damage convictions upheld after Jones.

enrichment.short_title: Ayliffe v DPP: Iraq protest aggravated trespass appeals dismissed

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: Three appeals concerned peaceful protests at military bases against the Iraq war in February and March 2003.
Protesters admitted aggravated trespass and, in two cases, criminal damage but argued disrupted activities were unlawful.
Defences relied on alleged crimes of aggression and possible ICC Act war crimes, plus section 3 prevention of crime.
District judges ruled the legality of the war and crimes against peace non-justiciable following Jones.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeals by way of case stated from magistrates' convictions for aggravated trespass and criminal damage at military protest sites.
enrichment.outcome: All appeals dismissed; convictions upheld because no sufficient issue was raised that war crimes were being committed and protests were not attempts to prevent crime.
enrichment.ratio: Following Jones, crimes against peace are not offences for section 68 lawful activity purposes; speculative ICC Act war crime assertions without evidence of specific offending on the land do not make port or base activities unlawful or support a section 3 defence where force was used to protest rather than prevent identified crime.
legal_issues: Whether crimes against peace made military activities unlawful under section 68(2)
Whether ICC Act war crime allegations were justiciable and required disclosure
Whether defendants used reasonable force under section 3 to prevent crime
Construction of section 68 and whether a distinct overt act existed in the Percy appeal
linked_authorities: R (Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament) v Prime Minister [2002] EWHC 2777 (Admin)

confidence.notes: Three consolidated appeals with detailed section 68 and Jones analysis and uniform dismissal.

notes: Internet venture fallout; Fletcher succeeded on company debt reimbursement but other claims failed.

enrichment.short_title: Fletcher v Davis: internet venture dispute and reimbursement claim
key_facts: Fletcher and Davis formed PFI in 1999 to develop Fletcher's internet advertising software idea with Davis providing capital.
A website launched in April 2001 but the founders fell out and the venture collapsed within months.
Fletcher claimed remuneration, wrongful removal as director, reimbursement of company debts and breach of a shareholders' agreement.
PFI was insolvent; patent applications lapsed and the copyright counterclaim was settled during trial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery trial of claims and counterclaim arising from the breakdown of a software joint venture between founder shareholders.
enrichment.outcome: Fletcher's reimbursement claim allowed; other claims against Davis dismissed and no order on the settled counterclaim.
enrichment.ratio: Where a founder paid identifiable company debts at the company's request or with its authority, he may recover reimbursement from the company despite the venture's failure; broader loss-of-profits and shareholders' agreement claims failed on the facts.
legal_issues: Whether a December 1999 shareholders' agreement existed and was breached
Whether Fletcher was wrongfully removed as a director
Whether Fletcher was entitled to reimbursement for company debts he paid
Whether Fletcher or Pages was the proper trading vehicle and ownership of the software

confidence.notes: Long fact-heavy judgment with clear partial success on reimbursement and dismissal of other heads.
